title: Time Doesn't Exist, and the Universe Didn't Come from Nothing
dek: Cosmologist Brian Keating makes a counterintuitive case: time may not exist, and the universe didn't arise from nothing. He also warns that AI can't replicate human intuition and can't be fully controlled.
why: This episode covers cosmology, dark matter, AI's limits, and trust in science. It's dense but personal in its views, ideal for listening during a commute or a run.
who: Tech founders, AI engineers, scientific skeptics, and anyone who wants a half-hour overview of cosmology and AI's boundaries.
skip: If you only care about AI, you can skip 27:08–35:14 on the early universe and the naming of weekdays.

points.h: Time doesn't add up, maybe because it doesn't exist
points.body: Keating argues that physics can explain space, matter, and energy, but not why time behaves as it does—possibly because time doesn't exist at all. He quotes Frank Wilczek's definition, "Time is what clocks measure," calling it a tautology. The real question he studies is "What happened on the Sunday before the Big Bang?"—how time emerged from nothing.

points.h: The universe didn't come from nothing: equations don't instantiate things
points.body: Keating directly refutes Lawrence Krauss's claim that the universe came from nothing as nonsense. Equations describe things but don't instantiate them. He asks what existed before the Big Bang—perhaps a previous universe or an eternal energy field, but definitely not "nothing." This statement is the key to understanding his entire argument.

points.h: Government canceled the South Pole array; only one similar experiment remains, in Chile
points.body: With the cancellation of the BICEP array in Antarctica by the U.S. government, the Simons Observatory at 5,200 meters altitude in Chile is now the only project of its kind still collecting data. It generates about 1TB of data per day, analyzed by 450 scientists, and is powered by solar panels for the first time. Keating's team is using it to make a decisive measurement of the cosmological time field.

points.h: Detecting primordial gravitational waves would rule out all other universe models
points.body: If primordial gravitational waves are detected, it would strongly support inflation theory while excluding all other models, such as an eternal universe, cyclic universe, eventual evaporation, or black hole origins. Keating stresses this isn't a final proof, but like Newton's laws being sufficient to guide moon landings, such evidence would still be powerful.

points.h: Lawmakers claim non-human beings exist but never show evidence
points.body: Keating criticizes the UAP field for its extremely low information environment. Despite authoritative figures like Congresswoman Luna claiming non-human beings exist, no physical evidence has ever been presented. He argues that if real evidence existed, it would have been made public by now; otherwise, it's a waste of public attention.

points.h: AI has been trained to be an apology machine, internalizing self-denigration
points.body: Responding to Peter's concerns about distrust in the state and science, Keating argues that Britain has contributed enormously to the Earth, yet Britons leave. He criticizes judging Churchill and Newton by today's standards and points out that AI has been trained to be an "apology machine," refusing to answer certain physics questions. He insists we must stop apologizing for human greatness, or AI will internalize self-denigration.

points.h: LLMs are just matrix multiplication; they can't invent chess
points.body: Keating explains that LLMs are based on matrix multiplication (linear algebra), not advanced mathematics; GPUs were originally optimized for gaming, not superintelligence. He gives examples: LLMs can't invent chess or the Rubik's cube; they only build on existing human data. He cites Jevons' paradox: the more AI is used, the lower the cost but the higher the usage. LLMs can't train themselves—they degrade like mad cow disease—and need new human data.

points.h: The real risk isn't AI running wild; it's that we can't live without it
points.body: Keating raises two major concerns: we don't understand how AI works, and we can't predict or control it. He references Turing's halting problem as an analogy for AI's unpredictability. His bigger worry is that if the AI bubble bursts (e.g., OpenAI losing $10 billion a month), humanity would be paralyzed by over-reliance.
